paper_title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: As AI conference submissions grow exponentially, the demand for reviews grows at the same rate (Kim et al., 2025; Ryu et al., 2025). Since the number of qualified human reviewers is limited, large language models (LLMs) are being considered as complementary paper reviewing assistants. Prior work proposes several AI reviewer training methods (Idahl and Ahmadi, 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). These studies formulate paper reviewing as *Corresponding authors. 1 holistic review-and-score generation to (1) maximize review quality relative to reference human review and/or (2) minimize the discrepancy between generated and human overall scores. This is essentially human review imitation problem. Training AI reviewers beyond human review imitation requires understanding the fundamental purpose of paper reviewing and defining an objective function that captures it. According to TMLR (2026), there are three main purposes of paper reviewing: evaluating papers soundness, interestingness, and clarity. Here, soundness refers to whether the claims made in paper are supported by accurate and convincing evidence and is the most important criterion. The other two criteria are more subjective and therefore need to be treated carefully. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating the soundness of papers with AI reviewers. To identify an objective function for the paper soundness assessment task, we conduct human study1 with seven AI researchers and identify two universal evaluation criteria (i.e., objectives): soundness2 and substantiveness, formally defined as follows. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PaperCritic on the in-domain PaperSound-23K test set and four out-of-domain (OOD) benchmarks covering Nature-family paper review, code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing. PaperCritic-4B outperforms other 4B models trained with conventional methods and frontier models on the in-domain dataset, and our RL training on ICLR paper reviewing consistently improves the models performance on all four benchmarks. We further show that our training method remains effective when using different LLM grader for evaluation and when training larger model. Our key contributions are: 1. We introduce the task of paper soundness assessment and formalize it as maximizing two objectives: (1) precision based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points and (2) coverage of reference points. 2. We build PaperSound-23K, large-scale dataset for training AI reviewers to assess the soundness of papers. 3. We propose simple training recipe including RL with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward that produces PaperCritic, which outperforms models trained with conventional methods and frontier models on the in-domain test set and effectively generalizes to four outof-domain benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Paper Review Datasets. Several studies have constructed paper review datasets by collecting paper drafts and expert-written reviews from different venues. Some early studies (Kang et al., 2018; Dycke et al., 2023) target preliminary tasks such as paper acceptance classification or review score prediction but do not cover full review generation. In contrast, more recent datasets (Gao et al., 2024; Weng et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025) are constructed specifically for the review generation task. Two important considerations are that reviewers have varied purposes when writing reviews and that the multiple points within review can vary in quality. However, the aforementioned datasets do not account for these two factors and primarily focus on collecting reviews at scale for model training. To Figure 1: Comparison of paper soundness assessments with conventional holistic review-and-score generation. Conventional AI reviewers are trained using holistic review similarity or preference and score similarity as objectives. In contrast, our learning objective is to jointly maximize (1) the soundness and substantiveness of review points and (2) the coverage of sound and substantive reference review points. sound and substantive) reference assessments. We treat soundness and substantiveness as the precision term and completeness as the recall term, and formulate paper soundness assessment as jointly maximizing precision and recall (Figure 1). To train AI reviewers to assess the soundness of papers, we construct quality-labeled review point dataset named PaperSound-23K. We sample 1K ICLR submissions and collect 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. To evaluate the quality (i.e., soundness and substantiveness) of these review points, we automate the process using an LLM with strong reasoning ability and observe human-model agreement comparable to human-human agreement  (Table 1)  . We train PaperCritic on PaperSound-23K training set through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sound and substantive reference points, followed by online reinforcement learning (RL) with an F1 reward. Two reward models (RMs) assess soundness address these issues, we narrow the scope of paper reviewing to paper soundness assessment and construct PaperSound-23K by labeling the quality of collected review points according to Definition 1. AI Reviewer Training. Another line of work explicitly trains specialized reviewer models. Idahl and Ahmadi (2025), Weng et al. (2025), and Zhu et al. (2025) train generic reviewing models by applying SFT to datasets of human-written or LLMsynthesized reviews. Zeng et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2026) also train generic reviewing models, but apply online RL to further improve review quality. These studies use holistic review similarity or preference relative to human reviews, together with overall score similarity, as rewards for model training. However, these methods provide sparse supervision and remain limited to imitating human reviews. Our work addresses these limitations by using evaluations of individual review points to provide dense rewards and defining new training objective. In addition, Mun et al. (2026) trains constructive feedback generators by applying SFT and DPO using author responses as quality labels for reviews. However, author responses provide noisy labels of review quality (Goldberg et al., 2025) and are difficult to use for online reward computation. We instead identify reliable review quality criteria under our problem formulation and use corresponding reward models that enable online learning.

sections.title: 5 PaperCritic Training Framework
sections.content: We train PaperCritic on PaperSound-23K with SFT on sound and substantive reference points (Section 5.1), followed by online RL using reward that combines precision and recall (Section 5.2; Figure 2).

sections.title: 5.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning
sections.content: We train PaperCritic with SFT on sound and substantive review points. Since review points are collected as an unordered set for each paper, we specify their order to construct training targets. To do this, we impose claim-diversity-aware order. We first group sound and substantive review points by their target claims and then interleave points across different claims whenever possible9. sections.title: 5.2 Online Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: Following the learning objective for paper soundness assessment (Section 3), we introduce an online RL training method by specifying (1) how to estimate precision and recall and (2) how to combine them into single reward. Given paper, the policy generates complete review as list of review points. We evaluate individual points rather than scoring the review holistically. Precision Estimation. We use separate RMs for soundness and substantiveness, evaluating each criterion on the corresponding scoring scale described in Section 4.1. The soundness RM receives the paper and the generated review point and examines whether the factual premises underlying the review point are supported by the paper or applicable domain knowledge. Only points whose material premises are supported (i.e., soundness score 2) are considered sound. For substantiveness, we provide the paper and its pre-extracted target claims with supporting evidence: routing stage selects the relevant claim, after which the substantiveness RM evaluates claim linkage and severity scores relative to that claim on 4-point scales. review point is substantive when both scores are at least 2. Review points that are both sound and substantive contribute to the precision numerator. Recall Estimation. An LLM matcher compares each generated point with the reference sound and 5 substantive points (from PaperSound-23K) and returns matched reference points. We follow the definition of matching in DArcy et al. (2024), which requires both high semantic relatedness and sufficient specificity: the generated point must express essentially the same criticism and be at least as specific as the reference. Each reference contributes at most once to recall. F1 Reward. We combine the estimated precision and recall into an F1 score and use it as review-level reward. The harmonic mean encourages balance between generating sound, substantive criticism and covering reference concerns: high precision alone cannot compensate for low recall, or vice versa. This scalar is assigned to the complete generated review and used as reward to update the current policy using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).

sections.title: 6 Experiments
sections.content: Our experiments address four research questions: (RQ1) How does PaperCritic compare with conventional reviewer-training methods and frontier models in automated and human evaluations? (RQ2) Does training on ICLR submissions generalize to other scientific domains and reviewing tasks? (RQ3) How do individual reward components and reward design choices affect performance? (RQ4) How robust are the observed gains across evaluation graders and policy models?

sections.title: 6.1 Setup
sections.content: Training. We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-8B (non-thinking) (Yang et al., 2025) as base policy models and train them on PaperSound-23K training set. We report hyperparameters and implementation details in Appendix C. Evaluation. We evaluate in-domain performance on the PaperSound-23K test set and OOD generalization on PeerReview Bench (Kim et al., 2026), which tests the ability to review Nature-family papers across the physical, biological, and health sciences. We also evaluate on SWE-PRBench (Kumar, 2026), CLAUSE-Legal (Choudhury et al., 2026), and StoryFeedback (Rashkin et al., 2025), which test performance on other reviewing tasks: code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing, respectively. We mainly report macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1, except for StoryFeedback, where we report only macro recall (i.e., the error detection rate), following the original work. For PeerReview Bench, we slightly adapt the evaluation protocol to our problem formulation so that the model reviews only the main paper. Detailed OOD evaluation is described in Appendix D.2. We use GPT-5.4, strong frontier model, as an LLM grader to automate these evaluations. We also conduct an exploratory human preference study comparing PaperCritic with frontier model at the review and review-point levels. Baselines. We compare against three types of AI reviewers for assessing paper soundness. (1) Models trained with conventional methods. For fair comparison with PaperCritic-4B, we use the same base model and train it using SFT (Weng et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025) and RL with different rewards, including preference reward (Zeng et al., 2025), based on holistic preference relative to human review, and similarity reward (Liu et al., 2026), based on the ROUGE score against reference review. We also train model using DPO (Mun et al., 2026), but use soundness and substantiveness pairs consistent with our problem formulation. (2) Larger/reasoning models from the same model family. We include Qwen3-32B and Qwen3235B with or without thinking (Yang et al., 2025). (3) Frontier models. We use DeepSeekV4-Flash-0731 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), Gemini 3 Flash (Google, 2025), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026a), Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a), with high reasoning effort. Reward models and matcher selection. We use GPT-5.4-distilled Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 model as the soundness RM and Qwen3.6-35BA3B as the substantiveness RM and matcher. Appendix provides the detailed selection process.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduce PaperCritic, an AI reviewer trained to assess the soundness of papers. We first formally define paper soundness assessment as jointly maximizing the precision of review points based on soundness and substantiveness and the recall (i.e., coverage) of reference points. Then, we automatically construct PaperSound-23K, quality-labeled review point dataset, using LLMs. We train PaperCritic models on this dataset, including through RL with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. The experimental results show 8 that our model outperforms baselines on the indomain dataset and effectively generalizes to OOD reviewing tasks.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Scope of paper reviewing. We intentionally restrict the scope of AI reviewing to assessing paper soundness. We do not explicitly optimize for other important purposes of peer review, such as interestingness, clarity, novelty, or the overall accept/reject recommendation, since several of these criteria are inherently more subjective. Consequently, PaperCritic should be viewed as an assistant for identifying soundness-related concerns rather than complete replacement for human peer reviewers. In addition, we exclude review points that rely on external citations and evaluate papers primarily from the information contained in the target paper. Real-world reviewing often requires comparing submission against related literature or external domain knowledge, which remains outside the main scope of this work. Incomplete reference coverage. Our recall objective relies on set of sound and substantive reference review points. However, neither humanwritten nor LLM-generated reviews can exhaustively enumerate all valid concerns about paper. Therefore, an unmatched generated review point is not necessarily incorrect or unhelpful, and our reference-based recall should be interpreted as coverage of known high-quality concerns rather than absolute completeness.

sections.title: Soundness Assessments
sections.content: Human study process. We recruit two research scientists and five PhD students, where the qualifi11 cation criterion is more than 3 years of AI research in their fields, which span on reinforcement learning, natural language processing, machine learning theory, computer vision, and speech processing. Once we recruit human experts, we randomly sampled 100 submissions in ICLR 20202023 for each human expert based on their relevant fields and let them select the most relevant work. Then, human experts spend 2 hours for evaluating overall quality of given review points on 5-point scale and justifying their evaluations. Based on this annotation, we also let them to write evaluation criteria of paper soundness assessments. Once we collect the annotations, we find that we additionally need to clarify the exact meaning of human experts justifications, so we conduct 1 hour of interviewing for every human expert and analyze their responses. Results. We first filtered out human experts justifications where they assume paper reviewing not as assessing soundness of papers, which includes assessing interestingness, novelty, or clarity of papers or providing constructive feedback. Then, we observe two universal and complete criteria that all human experts have: (1) Soundness. They give low quality score if review point contains an incorrect premise or its claim is not sufficiently supported by evidence (i.e., review point is unsound). During interviewing, we also confirm that high-scoring review points are all sound. (2) Substantiveness. They give high quality score if review point raises critical concern on the papers main claims (i.e., review point is substantive). We finally confirm that all high-scoring review points are sound and substantive and no lowscoring review points are sound and substantive. As result, we use these two evaluation criteria as an objective of assessing soundness of papers. A.2 Evaluating Review Point Quality Human annotation process. We recruit three PhD students who did more than 3 years of AI research in their fields. Once we recruit human annotators, we give them randomly sampled 100 submissions in ICLR 20202023 and they select total seven submissions. Then, they annotate soundness and substantiveness of human-written and LLMgenerated review points of the selected seven submissions. Specifically, we follow the same scoring scale described in Section 4.1. Since our goal includes measuring humanhuman agreement, all three humans annotate the same review points. sections.title: D Baselines and Evaluation Details
sections.content: D.1 Inputs, Inference, and Output Lengths Instructions and input content. All in-domain models review the same papers using the same core instruction: produce numbered list of sound, substantive criticisms that could undermine main claim, excluding novelty and minor presentation concerns. Inputs contain the papers title, abstract, and section text, without reference reviews. However, the prompts and available context are not strictly identical. Trained SFT/DPO/RL models use the original SFT instruction and 14,336-token input cap, retaining the paper prefix after reserving instruction/template space; four papers are truncated. Unadapted base, larger-Qwen, and frontier models receive the full rendered input, with additional instructions to produce at most eight points and target 100 words per point, and never exceed 132 words per point. This selection is made for fair comparison with the trained models; 100 words are an average number of words of PaperCritic-4Bs retained review points, and 132 words are their 97.5th-percentile length. 13 Decoding and parsing. Generation is one-shot. Local settings are temperature 0.7, top-p = 0.8, top-k = 20, repetition penalty 1.0, and base seed 42. API runs request the same temperature, topp, top-k, and seed where supported. Thinking is disabled for trained and base models; larger Qwen models are tested in both modes, and frontier models request high reasoning effort. Completion caps are listed in Table 11; API budgets may include hidden reasoning. The parser removes reasoning wrappers and code fences, splits numbered/bulleted items with their continuation lines, and retains only the first eight points. The trained-model parser additionally permits paragraph/line fallbacks and retains duplicates. The length-controlled suite requires list formatting and validates retained-point length, exact duplicates, and leaked reasoning, allowing up to two standard repair retries. It does not truncate individual points or select responses by review quality. D.2 OOD Evaluation Shared inference settings. Base Qwen3-4BInstruct-2507, SFT, and PaperCritic receive identical inputs and domain instructions within each benchmark. They generate numbered lists without per-point word limit; only the first eight points are evaluated. Thinking is disabled, top-k = 20, repetition penalty is 1.0, and the seed is 42 plus the instance index. PeerReview Bench and SWEPRBench use temperature 0.7, top-p = 0.8, and 16,384-token input cap; CLAUSE-Legal uses 0.6, 0.9, and 24,576; StoryFeedback uses 0.6, 0.9, and 8,192. Inputs are prefix-truncated when necessary, with legal authority text reserved in full. Completion caps increase from 2,048 to 4,096 and then 8,192 only after length cutoff. Remaining cutoff outputs and duplicate points are retained. PeerReview Bench. We evaluate the fixed first 50 papers (IDs 150), with 473 reference review items. Models receive main-paper text and available figure captions, without image pixels or supplementary files, and the same paper soundness instruction as in-domain generation. GPT-5.4 grades precision as the fraction of points rated Correct, Significant, and supported by Sufficient evidence. Reference coverage requires generated point with the same subject and argument, allowing different evidence. References requiring appendix information are not excluded: all 473 items remain, despite main-paper-only model inputs. SWE-PRBench. We use the eval_split configuration of foundry-ai/swe-prbench, with 598 human comments. Models receive PR metadata and the diff, without repository browsing. The prompt requests concrete correctness, reliability, security, performance, or integration issues grounded in the supplied change, not style-only criticism. The saved judge is GPT-5.4, receiving generated/human comments and up to 12,000 characters of selected diff. Precision is the fraction of generated comments classified as CONFIRMED against human issue; plausible but reference-unmatched issues do not count. Recall measures human comments classified as CAUGHT. CLAUSE-Legal. We use seed-42 sample of 100 positively annotated perturbed contracts: 50 CUAD and 50 ContractNLI. The reference sets contain 298 legal perturbations. The prompt requests contractlaw conflicts and additionally supplies each relevant law_citation and scraped_snippet_1; perturbation explanations are withheld from generation. One GPT-5.4 call per nonempty review performs many-to-many matching using generated points and reference perturbation descriptions, including available explanations, justifications, and law evidence. Precision is the fraction of generated points matched to at least one reference; recall counts uniquely covered references. 42 use 100 seed with sampled corrupted from StoryFeedback. We inputs igen/data/generated_feedback.jsonl, spanning 92 original stories; uncorrupted inputs are excluded. The prompt requests grounded, specific, actionable feedback on story coherence, clarity, fluency, style, or needed additions/deletions, permitting The text is perfect as-is. GPT-5.4 evaluates the entire feedback list. There is no point-level reference set or reported precision: the reported recall score is binary error detection, indicating whether any feedback addresses the biggest problem. I.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning We adapt the same point selection and claimdiversity-aware ordering used for one-shot SFT to construct next-point prediction examples. For an ordered sequence (p1, . . . , pm), we construct examples (x, ) p1, (x, p1) p2, ... (x, p1, . . . , pm1) pm. We additionally construct <STOP> target after the complete target sequence has been supplied. This terminal example is omitted when the sequence has been truncated by the maximum-point limit, so that truncation is not incorrectly treated as exhaustion of useful feedback. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the target point or stop signal, with the paper and preceding points serving only as conditioning context. The claim-diverse ordering is resampled across training epochs. I.2 Recursive Reinforcement Learning Starting from the recursively trained SFT model, we alternate between state-buffer construction and GRPO optimization. For buffer construction, we take batch of training papers and sample one recursive trajectory per paper using the current policy, holding its parameters fixed during this phase. At each step, we store the paper, its generated prefix, and the referencecoverage information associated with that prefix. Nonterminal points are appended without filtering them by reward, allowing subsequent states to include imperfect model-generated feedback. matcher identifies reference points covered by each sampled point and updates the remaining-reference set for subsequent states. Trajectories continue until the stop signal or the generation limit. We then train on the collected states. For each state, the current policy samples group of candidate next actions, which receive point-wise rewards and are optimized using GRPO. These candidates are newly sampled responses, rather than the responses previously used to construct the buffer. All candidates in group are evaluated against the same prefix and remaining-reference set; matching one candidate does not remove references for its siblings. After updating the policy on the buffer, we construct new buffer using the updated policy. Thus, RL uses model-generated rather than reference-written prefixes, with periodic refreshes of the training-state distribution.
